utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Smiljanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Visnjic will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your evidence to speak the truth continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let me remind you of our discussion on Friday when I showed you the collegium held on the 6th of November, 1998, that's Exhibit 3D664, and a part of the -- our discussion where you explained to us General Dimitrijevic's assessment related to the current situation in Kosovo and Metohija, or rather, that the security forces had withdrawn and that the KLA had already taken some territory and facilities and his assessment about future developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like this same document to be brought up on e-court, page 7, paragraphs 5 and 6 in B/C/S and page 6, or rather, 7, paragraph 1 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, after General Dimitrijevic spoke, General Marjanovic took the floor. What was his post at the time, General Marjanovic's?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I think that he was the chief of the artillery administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you if you see the document in front of you in e-court.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I seem to have a problem because I don't have it in front of me, so let us try -- I have it, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment on what General Marjanovic said, particularly the second paragraph beginning with the words: "In my view, this indicates that the assessment that they would wait for spring was correct ..."

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General Marjanovic confirms and is in agreement with the assessment presented by General Dimitrijevic about the return of the terrorist forces into the area abandoned by the security forces of Yugoslavia and they're reconstituting, re-arming, and preparations for possibly some larger-scale actions. And he notes, just as General Dimitrijevic did, that his assessments and the assessments made by General Dimitrijevic, that they would wait for the spring and that there would be a large-scale offensive in spring on part of the terrorist forces in Kosovo and Metohija were correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, but both Generals Marjanovic and Dimitrijevic, they make certain proposals as to how the army should respond, given the situation.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic and General Marjanovic in the situation that they faced made a proposal that the General Staff should address the relevant authorities in the state and ask that the verifiers of the OSCE mission should abide by the agreement, that they should not be biased, and that they should bind the other side to abide by what they had accepted in the agreement with the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we have page 8 in the B/C/S version and page 7 in English, last paragraph for the Judges to see, and then page 8 in English. Could we now have page 8 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, General Perisic did not attend this collegium meeting. When General Perisic was not present, who chaired the collegium?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of the General Staff was not present at the meeting. In this case and Colonel-General Dragoljub Ojdanic, the deputy Chief of Staff chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could we please comment on what General Ojdanic said here, that is the second paragraph of his intervention, beginning with the words: "Secondly, I absolutely agree with and support the proposal that we should, from our point of view, to the best of our abilities, demand a more vigorous reaction on the part of the international community regarding the fulfilment of the assumed obligations and agreements by the other side." So if you have anything to add or perhaps a comment on this paragraph or does it speak for itself?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it speaks for itself, certainly, but I can comment by saying that General Ojdanic agreed with the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, which means that the entire General Staff was in agreement. He supported General Dimitrijevic's and General Marjanovic's assessments and made a proposal to the competent authorities in the General Staff that they should intervene with the state authorities to intervene with the international community in order to force the other side to abide by or comply with the obligations they agreed to in the agreement with the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to quote anymore from this document, Your Honours, but I would likely to point to paragraphs 2 and 3 in the English text on page 8 that contain parts of General Ojdanic's intervention at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, now let us move on to another topic that we could perhaps tie-in with this collegium --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to be leading evidence of what was actually done as a result of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can partially lead evidence about what was actually done up until -- as far as the army is concerned, and later for that part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The real evidence in this situation is surely what communication there was as a result with the KVM. You can talk till the cows come home among yourselves, but what was actually done about it is the most significant thing. Was anything done? Perhaps the witness knows. Mr. Smiljanic, was anything done as a result of this agreement that you all came to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot claim that it was a direct consequence of this conversation, but definitely there were many such conversations in November and the consequence was the fact that General Milorad Obradovic, who was the chief of our team for cooperation with the OSCE mission, I know that he testified here already, sometime in the beginning, in the first half of December, he notified the collegium that the head of the state commission for cooperation with NATO, Mr. Sainovic, had convened an extraordinary meeting with the western European ambassadors accredited in Belgrade, and the topic was to be a debate about the conduct of the verifiers and the conduct of the other side, and by that they meant the terrorist forces in Kosovo, or rather, the agreement that had been signed on the 17th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may add, it is our position that even a discussion about that indicates intent and could be taken as evidence regardless of what actually happened later. We believe that even a discussion on this topic is quite significant and serves as an indicator of the existence of the intent on the part of the participants in this conversation on how things should proceed, how they should be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may be right, Mr. Visnjic, but if there was a document submitted to the KVM following a meeting like this we wouldn't need to go through the meeting, we would just need the document, because it would prove everything; but as it is, there isn't such a simple document. Anyway, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this is a very difficult question for me at this stage, but we will try to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let us just move on to another topic briefly, but perhaps this collegium might be a good reason to do so. An incident is mentioned as the collegium meeting proceeds involving a NATO aeroplane and since this is an area of your expertise could you please tell us briefly what this was all about and let me ask you at the same time the Yugoslav Army had signed a certain agreement with NATO about the verification that, in fact, regulated the use of air-space; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. On the 15th of October the army, or rather, the state of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia signed an agreement with NATO on the use of air-space above Kosovo and Metohija, and 25 kilometres into the depth of Serbian territory from the administrative border with Kosovo and Metohija on the part of surveillance aircraft of the NATO alliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this agreement was signed by General Perisic, but if I understand you correctly it was signed on behalf of the federal state of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Perisic signed this agreement as the -- General Clark and general did it on behalf of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, you answered in part what it was all about, but what was the obligation undertaken by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was tendered by the Prosecution as P450. We do not have it on our exhibit list, but we will be tendering it as a bar table exhibit. Let me just give you this information if it is necessary for any further proceedings involving this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what were the obligations undertaken by NATO and by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia under this agreement?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia under this agreement ceded the air-space over Kosovo and Metohija and 25 kilometres into the depth of the Serbian territory from the administrative border with Kosovo and Metohija for, conditionally speaking, unimpeded flight of NATO surveillance aircraft, U-2 aircraft flying at high altitudes, drones flying at lower altitudes, and surveillance aircraft flying at low and medium altitudes. The obligation undertaken by Yugoslavia was that when NATO aircraft flew over Kosovo and Metohija, including the safety zone, that the aircraft of the socialist -- of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not to fly, that all acquisition and guidance -- rocket-guidance radar systems should be switched off in the overall territory the Republic of Yugoslavia and that NATO could have priority in choosing their flight paths, their flight times, and they should have priority in air-space, as it is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So these were the obligations undertaken by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. What were NATO's obligations?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had to, as far as all the rocket air-defence systems, air-defence systems, and all systems, fire-control systems using radar data, to remove from Kosovo and Yugoslavia -- Kosovo and Metohija all such systems or to concentrate them and store them in a single facility and to report this storage site where all the rocket systems using -- used in air defence including light artillery, anti-aircraft -- anti-aircraft, light artillery, using radar data for fire control.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That was about the commitments of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and what about NATO's commitments, if any?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO had the commitment to announce their flights. There would be a weekly schedule, flight schedule drawn up. NATO picked their times for their flights. They had to leave six to eight hours open for the Yugoslav federal planes to use the air-space over Kosovo; however, in case of any emergencies their own change of plan, perhaps bad weather or something like that, within -- at a half-hour notice they had the right to change their flight schedule, making it impossible for Yugoslav planes to use the air-space.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, how did the implementation of this agreement go?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to implement the agreement and monitor the implementation of the agreement, two teams were set up. One was a NATO team headquartered at the headquarters of the air force and anti-aircraft defence and the other was the anti-aircraft defence team which was headquartered at the NATO headquarters, operative headquarters, in Vicenza. There was coordination between the two teams, there was exchange of information, and changes were sometimes announced, which made it possible for this agreement to be implemented with no major hindrances in purely relative terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 3D709.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, part of the agreement was that General Wesley Clark should visit the command of the air force on the 21st of December, 1998. What we see before us is a report that was produced in relation to this visit by Major-General Slavko Biga. Let's not dwell too long on this document. Can you just tell us what General Clark said on the implementation of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the agreement because right after this visit I took up duties of commander of the air force and air defence. It was conveyed to me at the time and I can now see for myself, that General Clark spoke in highly laudatory terms about our cooperation. He even invited the air force command to visit the operations centre in Vicenza. He did have a number of what you might call minor objections or remarks. He said that this sort of cooperation meant that there could be cooperation, but this form of cooperation left the entire air-space over Kosovo and Metohija entirely hamstrung for Yugoslav planes and it was no longer possible to train those planes at the Pristina airport. Given the weather conditions and the terms of the agreement, the fighters regiment at the Pristina airport remained grounded for nearly, nearly, five months. I also have to say that some air force equipment was used pursuant to that agreement -- yes, thank you. I also have to say that some anti-air force equipment or weapons that were kept in a particular location and were then moved were now placed under the strictest control of the OSCE verifiers. And our own people had access to the equipment for the purposes of training for technical inspection, but there had to be a 24-hour notice. And there was a ban on using radar systems, radiation radar systems, and also times when technical repairs were being carried out. Therefore, the agreement was high rest restrictive for the Yugoslav side, and to all practical intents immobilised the whole training system of the air force and air-defence forces in Kosovo for the period of time that the agreement prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the agreement continued to apply until the very beginning of NATO's aggression against Yugoslavia, did it not?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until the 20th of March when the NATO team left the air force headquarters, left the country altogether. It was only natural that the agreement should no longer apply. It was a day or two after their departure that a group of air force and air defence officers who had visited Vicenza, the operations headquarter, the NATO operations headquarters, came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 3D690, please. Your Honour, this is the Grom 3 directive, Thunderbolt 3. Can we please show page 3 of the B/C/S, paragraphs 4 and 5; English reference is page 3, paragraphs 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you as the air force and air defence commander, what did you think about NATO's involvement, the involvement of NATO's air force in terms of the prognosis in Thunderbolt 3, which is the first half of January 1999?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me and the entire air force command had a different approach, to some extent, to the aggression model than the one provided in this directive. However, there was a directive from the Supreme Command Staff which we ended up accepting. Our difference was in the fact that we were deeply convinced that should there be an aggression by NATO from the air-space, the entire territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would be attacked at once. We also believed that all the military potential and units throughout the area would come under attack. Furthermore, it was our assessment that somewhat larger forces would be used at first, especially cruise missiles, not just at first but also later, that these would be used to attack targets, which is the word very often used, throughout the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. When the aggression finally came, this proved to be true. From the very first minute, the very first bomb, the very first strike, there was a circular attack on the whole area of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with a slightly larger number of planes and cruise missiles than the assessment had predicted. Until -- and the consequences far outweighed the predictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let me try to remind you, you said this was a directive from the Supreme Command Staff; however, this is January 1999?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is this a directive from the Supreme Command Staff or the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the General Staff, my apologies. That was a slip of tongue on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we go to paragraphs 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Probable targets are mentioned here for the aggressor's air force. Without going into any great detail, tell me which territory this is about. Where are these facilities?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is only about Kosovo and Metohija. The only exception is the Kopaonik, the radar station at Kopaonik, which straddles the border of Kosovo and Metohija and facing Serbia, but you could say that it, too, is part of that same area, although it lies just outside it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So, General, what you predicted actually happened when NATO attacked Yugoslavia on the 24th of March, 1999, did it not? My first question in relation to that is: Which forces did NATO use when they first attacked the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I'm referring to the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, they had about 460 planes and 450 cruise missiles, and those were at the ready to begin the air-strikes. The very first night of the strikes, the first wave of strikes, about 150 planes were used and about 80 cruise missiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a difference in terms of how many weapons and forces were used at the beginning and at the end of these operations?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a huge discrepancy. There were, to begin, with 460 different types of planes used for different purposes. At the end, there were a total of 1.040 aircraft of all various types involved to carry out all sorts of different assignments. The original prediction was 450, and the 160 cruise missiles, that was the original prediction, but they still ended up firing over 1.000 cruise missiles at various targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what is the issue that this evidence goes to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this part of the witness's testimony is about a fact in a statement that the Defence stated in different forms, that one of the reasons for the movement of population was the NATO air-strikes. It is through this witness that I'm trying to familiarise the Trial Chamber with the extent of these air-strikes, the forces used, the structure of targets, and the type of weapons that Yugoslavia and Kosovo in particular were attacked with at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, how many flights were there and tell us about their structure, if you can, the NATO flights?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, there were about 26.000 flights altogether during the aggression on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. According to some NATO sources, the figure of 38.000 is one that is much bandied about; however, our information seems to suggest that the figure could be reduced to 26.000, of which 18.000 were carried out by fighter planes. A note-worthy feature was that in order to attack ground targets, 14.000 sorties were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, General. A total of how many attacks against the ground forces, Yugoslavia's ground forces and the targets on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the total of 14.000 sorties and air-strikes against the land forces, about 2.500 attacks were carried out. And just to explain this for the benefit of the Chamber, when I say an attack, this means an attack by a single plane or 100 planes, it makes to difference whatsoever. We're dealing with an attack in both cases. Therefore, a total of about 2.500 air-strikes and about 9.200 firings, cases of firing, against the ground forces and targets on the ground in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what sort of weapons were used during these attacks, General?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll put in what looser terms, but that's actually how it happened. With the exception of the nuclear bomb, all the other highly sophisticated state-of-the-art lethal weapons were used during the NATO air-strikes on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Let me mention a couple of these bombs of precise effective global positioning, long-distance or, better said, distance outside the range of our systems, the systems that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had at the time, and I'm referring to air defence systems; cluster bombs; shells used primarily to target forces in Kosovo and Metohija containing depleted uranium; graphite bombs, used to target sources of electricity and transmission systems; and other weapons, too, with a huge destructive potential approaching the destructive potential of low-power nuclear bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How many military targets would there normally be and how many civilian ones when an attack was carried out?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very first night, NATO started attacking civilian targets. The whole of the Rakovica industrial complex, including Belgrade's bread factory came under attack on the 24th of March in the first wave. Therefore, civilian targets were being attacked from day one. As of the beginning of April, civilian facilities came under attack every day and the intensity of these attacks was quite high. According to our information, there were about 3.380 and something cases of firing on civilian targets, which is about 36 per cent of all the firing that occurred during NATO's intervention in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; therefore, that was the breakdown. About 60 per cent military targets and about 40 per cent, globally speaking, I'm not being highly precise right now, 36, 37 per cent civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in what sectors and on what axes were most of these strikes carried out?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the strikes were carried out in the wider Belgrade region. When I say that, I mean that that was the greater intensity, the highest fire-power was used, the highest fire-power was there. The other sector that came under attack to a certain -- to a similar scale as in Belgrade was Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what zones and what axes in Kosovo and Metohija came under strike of NATO aircraft?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO aeroplanes mostly attacked the border area with Albania and Macedonia and the Djeneral Jankovic-Kacani-Urosevac-Pristina axis. In this area which is 20 to 30 kilometres into the depth of the Kosovo and Metohija territory from the border, about 80 per cent of all fire opened in Kosovo and Metohija was there, and there were three other municipalities in Kosovo and Metohija. So in this territory of all the facilities that were destroyed, 75 per cent of those facilities were in this area, the border area with Albania and Macedonia and the Djeneral Jankovic-Pristina axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are there any specific munitions that were used in this area?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was talking about the use of various military assets or munitions, but it is -- it must be noted that over 80 per cent of the depleted uranium rounds were used in this area. A large number of cluster bombs were used in this area, but the old method, the so-called old method of carpet bombing was applied here. Bomber aircraft released their bombs from 10.000 metres, B-52 aircraft, and bombs are dropped randomly over a large area, there is no targeting, and they hit -- they can hit anything on the ground. So in this area, this is where most of the action concentrated in Kosovo and Metohija and perhaps this then means that this was the highest ratio of actions in the entire territory of Yugoslavia, and most of the destruction happened there indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what was your assessment and can you tell us why this area was targeted to such a large extent?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our assessments and to my understanding there can be two reasons for that, perhaps more than two, but let me just present two. The first is that throughout the aggression there was a plan to launch a ground attack, to use ground forces, for an invasion. The area that came under such an attack was needed for a ground invasion by NATO troops in order to clear the troops from that area, thus facilitating their taking of this territory and using it as a base for further advances into Kosovo and Metohija and reaching the other border probably, that Prepolac and Kosovsko Pomoravlje, that's one of the reasons. The other reason was such attacks were designed to force the civilians to move. It is quite logical if there is such an attack, every normal human being seeks shelter from such attacks, and then the population was to move. And many in the western world condemned this aggression, many of the peace-loving people in western Europe and in the western sphere condemned this aggression, and in order to justify the aggression and to create an illusion among those people that there was a humanitarian disaster caused by the forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or rather, the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, could you please tell us in relation to the forces available to NATO and the Yugoslav air defence and air force, what was the ratio?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of equipment, the technological degree of development, it is impossible to compare, there can be no comparison. NATO forces really had an advantage that went beyond any comparison. In terms of figures, let me just give you an example which is really quite striking. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had ten fighter planes that could be used to fight a NATO aircraft according to their specifications. Their specifications were close to NATO aircraft specifications. And facing those ten aircraft in possession of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, NATO had 100. If we look at the number of sorties, that would be -- the Yugoslav air force and air defence aeroplanes had ten sorties and NATO aircraft 4.000 sorties, so that would be the ratio of 400:1. Numerical indicators are really frightening, if I may be so bold as to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us paint this picture for the Trial Chamber. The attack aircraft of NATO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that, can you clarify the figure you've given us about 4.000 sorties. We've -- the transcript earlier showed a figure of 14.000. What is the figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. 14.000 sorties, that's for ground attacks. That's assault aircraft that has the appropriate equipment and weapons to target ground targets. And there were 4.000 fighter aircraft sorties, fighters fight other fighters, so that was for the air fights against the fighters of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So that's an indicator, and these figures are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell us how many NATO aircraft would there be in the air-space daily? I don't know if you have any figures to that effect.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the air-space of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, daily 2.030 aircraft would get into that air-space, aircraft of various purposes, mostly aircraft designed to attack ground forces. Fighter planes didn't actually get into the air-space, they did it very rarely. They operated from the borders of the neighbouring countries. And it's interesting to note that in the course of intense negotiations about the cease-fire and the cessation of the aggression on the 26th of May, 535 NATO fighters entered the air-space above our country. It's a frightened figure because it's a small space, but it is interesting, too. Because at that time there were intense negotiations and an agreement was almost reached, yet this is the time when so many aircraft take off to target ground targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to correct the transcript, page 18, line 25, the figure there should be 232, not 2.300 [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in light of everything that you told us, was NATO hampered in terms of choosing weapons, quantity of munitions, times of attack on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, NATO did not face any restrictions in light of the -- its strength, the inferiority of the arms or equipment in possession of the air force and air defence. NATO could choose time, conditions, axes, and that's what it did. The aggression was carried out from a circular base from the territories of all the countries around us, and I have to stress that only in the second period did they launch attacks from the territories of Romania and Bulgaria.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. You were the commander of a strategic group. What was -- how -- to what extent were you independent or what was your discretionary right after you got the order from the Supreme Command Staff? To what extent were you guided in the use of the forces that you had or were you independent and to what extent in your decision to use the forces that you had been given?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had full independence, in short. A commander who is given an approval for his decision from the superior command or commander is entirely free to apply any models, methodology, time, definitely, if the decision does not limit the time, but he is completely free to choose how to carry out the task he was given. And in principle General Ojdanic - and that's a fundamental principle in our rules, the principle of the singleness of command, which determines that there should be one commander, one decision, one responsibility. Definitely after a decision has been approved no commander can start on a combat mission if the decision he had made was not approved by his superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. Now that you mentioned General Ojdanic, what option did General Ojdanic have when NATO made the decision to attack the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we please have Exhibit P1085, page in B/C/S 262 and English version that's page 216.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the only option that General Ojdanic had at the time was to defend his country against the outside aggression and against the armed rebellion from inside the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't understand -- I didn't understand the question, and General Ojdanic was not the supreme commander. So what is it you're really asking here?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Presumably his only option is to obey the man that commands him, do as he's told.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that is not in dispute, that that was the option, but I would like to bring to the fore one part that pertains to my next question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you and General Ojdanic, like all the other personnel of the army, you took an oath. Do you remember when did you take the oath?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was long time ago. I took the oath in the first year of air force academy after completing my basic training, that was in 1964, late 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, now when you look at this text, the text of this oath that you have in front of you, that is from the rules of service issued in 1996, is this text different in any essential way from the text that you took -- of the oath that you took in your time?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there may be some slight changes, but the essence of the oath remained the same and it really does read: "I swear by my honour and my life that I shall defend the sovereignty, territory, independence, and the constitutional order," in this case it's the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That's approximately the same oath that we took, but this is the one that is in force now. That's the valid one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. That would more or less complete your evidence, but I do have one brief question. Could you please tell me, what were the capabilities of the aviation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to operate during the NATO attacks to carry out any attack flights, attack missions?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, meager capabilities from the technical point of view, but also from the point of view of training. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as it is quite well-known, from 1992 until the aggression was under a blockade and very severe sanctions that affected all spheres of life of a state and of a people. In 1995, this regime became a bit more lax, but training in particular of the air force which uses up a lot of assets, that was down to a minimum. Pilots would have 25 to 30 hours, as opposed to 300 hours that would be NATO standard. So you cannot really compare it and that might be quite striking for anyone who was not familiar with those figures. As far as ordnance was concerned, the quantities were low and the air force aircraft could only carry out attack flights, attack missions, during the day because we didn't have weapons that could be used at night or in adverse weather conditions. So in terms of attack missions, our assets were very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to show a short video, it's under a minute long I think, and it's about the bombing of the village of Nogavac, which I'm sure you remember was mentioned by a number of OTP witnesses. I showed the General this footage, it's part of a large-scale compilation. We are using the portion that we believe is important for our analysis. I have shown the General this footage. He has gone through it, and I believe he'll be able to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's see it then. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an issue regarding foundation and authenticity. I don't know if the General took this video or if he's seen it, but so far from what I've been provided I can't tell where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've just been told he has seen it. The source of this, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I got this as part of a more extensive compilation. I got it from a Defence team in a different trial, and this wide-ranging compilation was about many events at the time, one of these being the village of Nogavac. As far as I know, it was a Zastava film that took this footage it's military service producing documents and films; however, if Mr. Hannis has any objections to raise about this I will try gradually to gather information to support the authenticity of this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding the wider compilation, I looked at the first 10 or 12 minutes seemed to be an interview with General Maisonneuve who testified here and then there were two or three minutes of some guys digging trenches and I don't know who they were or what they were doing. This is followed by somebody in a hospital. This is a mixed bag of things and I don't know where it comes from, that's why I raise the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the question you intend to request, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm waiting for -- [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just want to ask the witness whether he can comment, since in the footage we see part of a certain bomb or rocket or something, whatever, that's one thing; and the other thing is, given the form of the damage that occurred can he ascertain what weapon was used. There's nothing about the place or anything about that. I want his professional comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we'll allow this to be shown and the questions to be asked, but we will mark the exhibit for identification and we will reserve the question of the relevancy of the answers that are given until we're able to deal with the authenticity of the extract. So please proceed on that basis, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the film has started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the exhibit number, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is 3D710.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, briefly, no details, please, you've seen this footage a number of times, haven't you? We zoomed in on certain portions of this tape. Can you please tell us what you've just seen.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Large-scale destruction, to begin with. Part of a projectile that was supposed to be used; however, the amount of destruction caused does not correspond to that. In addition to that, there had to be something else being used, some other kind of weapon. I think even high-pressure weapons such as oxygen bombs, something like that, which creates a high atmospheric pressure and a large-scale explosion of pressure or a fragmentation missile such as a cluster bomb. If we could please rewind to that bit where we see the remains of a missile that was probably used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please focus on that. Yes, yes, that's what I mean. It is my inner-most conviction that this is a part of -- can we please not zoom out, leave it like that, especially where we see the writing. This is the rocket engine of a HARM 88 missile. You can see the writing in English. Were we to analyse this, we would soon learn what this means. This is the charge number, the fuse, the shelf-life, as it were, of the missile, it's all in English. And it is in my opinion that this was the missile used. Personally, I do believe that other kinds of weapons were used as well. I have to point out yet again, to the extent that I'm familiar with this and I am because I have been proofed for this testimony, I think that this operation took place, this attack took place, at 2.00 in the morning, two minutes past 2.00, on the 2nd of April. Our own air force did not have any crews trained for this sort of an attack. They didn't have weapons like this and they didn't have planes like this and they could certainly not carry out an attack at that time of night. They could have just dropped bombs randomly, of course, but I have to rule out the possibility because we simply weren't able to attack by night with the planes that we had. The only night-time planes that we had were fighter planes, but that was quite a meager crop altogether as the first night of the NATO aggression proved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, just another question, were you aware of any plan to relocate or expel the Albanian population from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other counsel wish -- Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If you -- with your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning and the rest of the day, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm Djuro Cepic. I will ask you two questions, a grand total of two questions on behalf of General Lazarevic. I'll talk about the air force and air defence in Kosovo and Metohija. So the question is: Were there any such units in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were air force and air defence units in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you name some, please, not all?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire Velika Slatina airport, today it's called Pristina airport, was a facility that was in the hands of the air force and air defence units. A fighter plane regiment was stationed at that airport and they had MiG-21 planes. The logistics were provided by a brigade-level unit for the air base, and there was also the 311th Rocket Regiment in Kosovo armed with a KUP system, and there was also a platoon stationed at Goles, just above Velika Slatina airport. Three higher-level tactical groups and one basic tactical group in Kosovo and Metohija from the air force and air defence altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have error in transcript, 27th page, line -- line 5, I think that the witness said that those units were in Kosovo and Metohija, just to distinguish units in the area of airport Slatina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Line 5 ... You mean line 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: 311 Rocket Regiment -- yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what are you saying is the problem? We can clarify it with the witness. Where is it you're saying the 311th Rocket Regiment was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 311th Rocket Regiment was stationed in the general Velika Slatina airport area. It wasn't at the airport itself. It was located in the general area in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My last question: Who was in command of this unit, these units?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Globally speaking, the command of the air force and air defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But some of the forces were in the anti-aircraft corps of the air corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other one was part of the air force and air defence corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I wanted to follow-up on one of the last --

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the last things you talked about. You mentioned NATO didn't have any hindrances on its abilities to carry out its attacks during the aggression, but there were several occasions where they were hindered by bad weather; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know and I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're not aware that there was some days when the number of sorties or missions were greatly reduced or didn't take place at all in some areas?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about weather, it was far less favourable for us, given the level of equipment that we had at our disposal. It is true that there were days that there were 535 sorties, such as on the 26th of May, and there were days when there were between 100 and 200 sorties. But I really can't say in relation to each of those 78 days, but there is information indicating that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And General Naumann from NATO was here in December and testified for us, and one of the things he told us in his testimony that the NATO air-strikes were also complicated by the Serb use of homes and buildings to hide weapons and vehicles as well as the intermixing of military vehicles with civilian convoys. Those are tactics that were sometimes used by the Serb army; is that true?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that it's true simply because I wish to say that the air force and air defence in its manoeuvres never used civilian convoys. It would be ridiculous to see a rocket-guiding radar among tractors or buses. Therefore, I can't confirm that, but I certainly doubt it very much. This would be an inhumane thing, and I can be quite certain, in fact, that VJ commanders never used anything like this, this sort of employ, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how can you be certain of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I know, I am nearly certain. Let's say I'm not 100 per cent positive; let's leave it at nearly certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were shown a video of some damage and what appeared to be a portion of some sort of missile or bomb. Can you tell us the first time you saw that video?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first watched it closely during my proofing, but I had seen it before in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was the first time you saw it in Serbia, if you recall, what year?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you certainly weren't out there on the scene where this video was taken, were you?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you don't have any personal knowledge of exactly where that was taken?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or when it was taken?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Or by whom it was taken?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attorney Visnjic told me that, but it's not something that I can speak to from personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. I'm just asking you about your personal knowledge. And you have no way of knowing whether or not that bomb fragment or that portion of the missile was in place or if it was brought and put there by someone else?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this may be analysed further, but if you have a close look there's a crater just next to this missile, the HARM 88 missile, and there's a crater which is very much like those left by these missiles in other places. For example, at the Batajnica airport, that's what I looked at one. The crater is nearly the same in terms of shape. Therefore, if you use the comparative method you can - or perhaps not depending on your skill - conclude that there's a likeness between the two. But I'm certain that a missile like this could not have caused this amount of destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you about Exhibit 3D669.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could bring that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is -- General, while it's coming up I'll tell you that this is an order from the General Staff, the first administration, to the commands of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd Army, to the air force, the navy, and the special units. And it apparently arises out of an extraordinary meeting of the collegium that had taken place on the 21st of February. Do you recall if you attended the collegium session on the 21st of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could first see what this is about, and then perhaps I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you see if you look at the header or the preamble, the air force and air defence commander reported on the combat-readiness and the situation in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was reviewed, the situation concerning the combat-readiness of the VJ --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is: Were you present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's just what I'm telling you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- That is indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the answer is yes. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to look at item number 15 in this order, General, and I have a question for you once we have that up on the screen. I've got my English but I don't think you have the B/C/S yet. Okay. Item number 15 is translated into English as: "Some of the requests filed by army and RM," which I understand stands for the navy, "by army and RM commanders, which are of a political nature and not under the jurisdiction of the General Staff of the VJ, will be sent to the relevant organs for processing." Do you recall what those requests by the army and navy commanders were that were of a political nature in this February extraordinary meeting?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, you're not really consistent in reading this paragraph, but it doesn't affect the substance. I think and I'm confident that there were no political demands being made, and I really can't say what this is about. The head of the information and morale guidance administration here is responsible for cooperating with state institutions dealing with morale and passing on information. He was given an assignment - and I really can't say what that assignment was - but one thing that I can say is that I myself raised no political requests whatsoever. It doesn't say belong to the domain of political demands, it says belong to the domain of a political nature. Everything is politics. War is politics too. Politics, I don't see any political demands being made here and it doesn't actually state that there were political demands being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That may have been a matter of translation, because the English says and what I read was: "Some of the requests filed by army and RM commanders, which are of a political nature and not under the jurisdiction of the General Staff ..." So my question is: You don't recall at the meeting two days prior any discussion about those kinds of things; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I can say that it is impossible to wage a war, to prepare for a war, without having political views. There would be a disharmony in the system and it would lead nowhere. I don't know and I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this a good time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll break here. Mr. Smiljanic, we have to break now for 20 minutes. Could you please leave the courtroom now with the usher and we'll see you again at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I wanted to ask you a question about General Grahovac. I understand -- was he the assistant to the Chief of General Staff for air and air defence forces in early 1999?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I have a note indicating that he was replaced about the 19th of April, 1999. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, frankly, I couldn't comment on it. This was up to the General Staff or the Supreme Command Staff, as it was at the time, about personnel appointments. I had nothing to do with that and I couldn't really comment on it. It's probably correct. I think that he actually got promoted to a higher post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But that happened -- that change occurred while the NATO bombing was still going on, correct, and you don't know why. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were any of your planes still flying in April and May of 1999 or had they all been put out of operation?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last flight, the aviation stopped flying on the 4th of April, but the last flight was on the 4th of May when a MiG-29 was scrambled to face a group of aeroplanes heading towards Serbia, but from that time on there were no more flights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can someone assist, is there an error in line 17? You've been recorded as saying, Mr. Smiljanic, that the aviation stopped on the 4th of April, but the last flight was on the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These seem to contradict each other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The aviation stopped flying on the 4th of April, but there was one single flight on the 4th of May. So you could say that the aviation stopped flying on the 4th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just to be clear then. After the 4th of April, there was one single occasion when one of your planes flew, and that was on the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier this morning when Mr. Visnjic was asking you a question about the collegium meeting on the 6th of November, 1998, you talked about the positions set forward by General Dimitrijevic and General Marjanovic and noted that General Ojdanic agreed with them, with their assessments, about making a proposal to the competent authorities that they should intervene with the state authorities to intervene with the international community in order to force the other side to abide by or comply with the obligations that they had agreed to in the agreement with the OSCE mission. My question is: In that context who are you referring to when you say "the other side"?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the Siptar terrorists in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I have a question for you. The Siptar terrorists or sometimes they're referred to as the KLA or the so-called KLA, they had not signed any agreement with Mr. Milosevic or Mr. Holbrooke, had they?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't comment on that, but you should look at the agreement between Zivadin Jovanovic and the OSCE president, I think it was Geremek.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But nobody from the KLA or the so-called KLA or the Siptar terrorists had signed that agreement either, had they?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That agreement was signed by the international community on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On behalf of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on behalf of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who in the KLA gave them authority to do that?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to ask somebody from the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And didn't -- didn't OSCE indicate that one of their problems was that they didn't have any control over the KLA because the KLA had not signed the agreement under which the KVM was operating?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, this was the problem for the OSCE, not for me and not for the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that regarding the NATO air-strikes in answering a question from Mr. Visnjic, I think you said that the air-strikes came generally in the areas that you had anticipated. Would that be fair? I'm not sure if you said that or not, but is it fair to say that based on your pre-war assessment the air-strikes came at the locations that you largely anticipated they would?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said, and it would be absurd and pointless to assess that the NATO would hit precisely the targets that we anticipated, but as for some key facilities in the overall territory and territory in general areas, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, maybe I should phrase it in terms of general targets. They generally struck at the kinds of targets you would expect them to in such an operation. Air defence, anti-aircraft defence, communications, command, weapons producing installations, et cetera, correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we anticipated, but we didn't anticipate that they would destroy the bridges on the Danube, the bread production facilities, that they would bomb water-supply plants, thermal electric plants, the oil industry facilities, historical monuments, cultural monuments, and so on and so forth. There were many other things that we didn't anticipate, but I don't want to bother you with all that. We anticipated that that would be war in which soldiers would fight soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the first couple of weeks of the war, weren't the strikes primarily at those kinds of targets, air defence, military installations and facilities, communications and control sites, and the attacks on infrastructure came later, right?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From day one there were attacks on infrastructure that had nothing to do with military facilities or facilities used to wage the war, such as, for instance, the Rakovica bread production plant near Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you have precise information about -- you've given us precise information about the number of sorties and the number of flights, the number of missiles, and you must have precise information about these -- the individual targets damaged, correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely not, but in general terms, yes. The damage was assessed by the competent state commission with the participation of the army and all the institutions of the state, they came up with an assessment of the damage. I don't think that I'm competent to discuss this damage assessment. There are people who participated in that exercise who would be much more competent to speak about it and to give you much more precise information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you were drawing the distinction between military targets and civilian targets, when you say civilian in this context you're really talking about non-military, you're not talking about residential housing areas, are you, or farming villages?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that does not serve the function of waging a war and everything that is not used to wage a war is -- for military purposes that's civilian facilities, and that's what I'm talking about, targets that are not used for the purpose of waging a war, they were targeted. Let me give you an example, my apologies to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Smiljanic, could you just please answer the question that you were asked, and that was whether residential areas and farming villages were bombed deliberately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that residential buildings were bombed, and if they were bombed that means that there was an intention to do so. It's -- you can't do things randomly. There must have been an intention and a purpose behind the bombing of those areas. We have Surdulica, Aleksinac, Belgrade, we have a number such examples, but I wanted to explain merely about the target selection. One day because of NATO air-strikes that hit water-supply system and the water-supply plant in Belgrade, Belgrade was left with 8 per cent of its water reserves, and we're talking about 2 million inhabitants. If the water-supply systems, the water reserves, and the water-supply plant, if that's a military facility then indeed they were justified in targeting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you explain to me the difference between a sortie and an attack. You mentioned there were 14.000 sorties flown. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A flight "polet" is a -- when an aircraft takes off and does not attack. Out of 14.000 flights, 9.200 opened fire, so 60 per cent of the aircraft entering the Yugoslav aircraft [as interpreted] actually carried out attacks and opened fire, so that's a difference between a combat flight and an opening of fire in a combat situation, firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I still need your help on the terms. You mentioned 14.000 sorties, 2.500 attacks, and 9.200 firings. Is -- a firing, is that an individual missile or a bomb? Does each one count as an individual firing?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Individual round missile, so that's an individual instance when an aircraft opens fire, just as we said that there were 14.000 individual sorties, there were 9.200 individual instances when weapons were fired, bombs were dropped, missiles were launched or any other ordnance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then I take it an attack is where there's been an sortie with an attack and one or more firings of a bomb or a missile or some sort of weapon, correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you can have an attack even when fire is not opened. You can attack and then somebody prevents you from actually opening fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, how do you determine that's an attack if no fire is opened?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, yes, fire is opened. An attack in which fire is opened. Well, apart from the indicators on the ground, you have to bear in mind that radio surveillance, radar surveillance, monitoring the entrance of aircraft and their movement also provided additional information about the number of attacks, the number of times when fire was opened, because first you have to determine that an aircraft entered the air-space, how many aircraft, and how many times fire was opened. So as we said, that's the figures we have and I already indicated that according to some US sources there were 36.000 to 38.000 of those combat flights.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, now that's a new term and a new number for me. What's the relationship between 36 to 38.000 combat flights and 14.000 sorties and 2500 attacks?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- 36.000, it's a mistake. It's 38.000, that's the correct figure, and that's from NATO sources and NATO analysis. That's the figure that they have. Now, if I have to explain to you what you just asked me, could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess what's the difference between a combat flight and a sortie in this context?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No difference. Sortie is part of a flight. If you take off, then you complete your flight. Combat flight, "borbeni let" is the correct term because it includes taking off, landing, and everything in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess you'll have to help me with this then. You told us there were 14.000 sorties; NATO says there were 38.000 combat flights. Where's the -- where are the other 24.000? Are those NATO planes that took off that didn't make it to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already explained this. I said our data indicate, we have data that NATO in the course of the aggression against Yugoslavia carried out 26.000 combat flights, and I added that according to some US sources there were 38.000 such flights. We don't have to accept that as relevant piece of information. Out of those 26.000 take-offs, 18.000 were combat flights and 7 or 8 or whatever it is to do the balance are assistant aircraft flights, AWACS, tank planes, and so on. Out of the 18.000 combat flights, 14.000 flights were used for ground attacks and 4.000 were carried out by NATO fighter planes. These are also combat flights. So it's 18.000 total. Out of 14.000 flights that attacked ground targets, 9.200 actually opened fire and 5.000, or rather, 4.800 did not. Those 9.200 instances when fire was opened occurred in a total of about 2.500 attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, there's a new number but I'm going to move on. You said at page 15, line 18 today that: "Most of the strikes were carried out in the wider Belgrade region, and when I say that I mean that that was the greater intensity the highest fire-power was used, the highest fire-power was there." So when you say most of the strikes were carried out in the wider Belgrade area, if we were talking about 9200 firings, how many of those were in the wider Belgrade area? Half? More than half? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you that information now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how much -- you mentioned that another sector that came under attack to a similar scale was Kosovo. Do you know what the proportion was between Belgrade and Kosovo? Did they both have about the same amount? Was it about half and half? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More attacks were carried out in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, that's what I stressed, than in the Belgrade area. But in the Belgrade area in terms of the strength of weapons and destruction, that was worse. There were large -- large industries there and strong fire-power was used there, highly destructive weapons were used. But there were more attacks in Kosovo but using less destructive weapons, such, as for instance, depleted uranium shells that have a high destructive power -- but have lesser destructive power, but the consequences are more far-reaching, more serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in regard to the follow-up question from Mr. Visnjic that with regard to Kosovo NATO aeroplanes mostly attacked the border area with Albania and Macedonia and the Djeneral Jankovic-Kacani-Urosevac-Pristina axis. In this area which is 20 to 30 kilometres into the depth of Kosovo about 80 per cent of all fire opened in Kosovo was there. And because you ran three places together, I'm not sure -- was 80 per cent of all fire opened in Kosovo in the Djeneral Jankovic-Kacani-Urosevac-Pristina axis or do you mean in the three areas including the Albania and Macedonia borders?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I include the border area facing Albania and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your theory for the reason why so much bombing took place in that area, you said there were two possible reasons and one of them you said was that the attacks were designed to force the civilians to move. So when did you come to the conclusion that the bombing at the border was to drive away the civilians? Was that right away in the first couple of days of the war or only after the end of the war or when did you decide that that was the reason?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to pin-point the time, but once it was observed that there were those intense attacks in this area using a lot of assets and knowing that there were talks, plans, for a ground invasion, one of the reasons was to destroy the military assets there, creating a favourable basis -- base for entering into the Kosovo and Metohija territory; and the second reason was surely, that was an assessment, that the western world had to get this picture of a humanitarian disaster caused by the Serbian forces making the Albanian population move and leave the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and the easiest thing to do was to make the people living in the border area move. Very few people moved from the Kosovsko Pomoravlje area because it was further away from the border, it would have been much more difficult. But in this area the situation was such that the people had to be made to move in order to create this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we've had evidence in this case from a lot of people all over Kosovo that the reason they moved and left was because they were driven out by the army and the police. Now, if you were aware or believed that the NATO bombing at the border was to drive the civilians out, why would you move civilians from the interior to the border in the line of fire of all this NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a complex and difficult question, but wherever you have bombs falling, nobody will just stand idly by and watch as the bombs keep falling. We had professionals flee these areas, too, let alone people who weren't trained, who really thought this was some sort of punishment falling from the sky or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, are you familiar with the geography and some of the major towns in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To quite a large extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Given your theory, do you know why hundreds or thousands of people, Kosovo Albanians from Kosovska Mitrovica would go halfway across Kosovo to the Albanian border if that's where the bombings were taking place?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when they did that and I really don't know why, but I don't know when it was that they moved from Kosovska Mitrovica towards the Albanian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. You mentioned that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had ten fighter planes that could be used to fight a NATO aircraft according to their specifications. Which ones were those? Were those the MiG-21s?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those were MiG-29s.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know when and where you had obtained those MiG-29s?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those planes were obtained from the Soviet Union back in 1987 and 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what about the MiG-21s, do you know when and where they were obtained?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a plane that was obtained from the Soviet Union, too, in the 1970s. This is a second-generation MiG. It was outdated, obsolete you might say, and it no longer had the appropriate features for a fighter intercepter plane, especially as compared to the opponent's fighter planes, which had missiles whose range was as far as 120 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're not aware of any MiGs obtained from the Russians at a later date after the embargo and the sanctions were in place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that at all. If there were any that were bought, I would have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're not aware of a trip that I think General Grahovac took with Mr. Lilic and someone else to see about buying some MiG planes?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a trip that occurred perhaps, I don't know, but it wasn't my responsibility to monitor Lilic's movements at the time, whatever his capacity was. He wasn't state president, but certainly there were no MiGs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what about General Grahovac, do you know about him going on that trip with Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It wasn't my job to look into this trip that they may have made or to wonder why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
