utterances.text: You mentioned the importance that General Ojdanic put on the general principle of singleness of command. Did you ever hear of a body in 1998 or 1999 called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And have you heard of it since 1999?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the Slobodan Milosevic trial, I heard of the existence of such a body, that a body like that existed or was rumoured to exist, which I doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we show the witness P1487, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That will come up on the screen in a minute, General. I'll tell you this is a document from the Supreme Command Staff, staff operations department. It's signed by General Ojdanic and it's dated the 17th of April, 1999, and it's to the commander of the 3rd Army who we know at the time was General Pavkovic. And it's entitled: "Suggestions." And it's linked to a document that we've seen in evidence in this court already called the Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command order, strictly confidential number 455-148 of 15 April 1999. Now, do you have any reason to doubt the authenticity of this document from the Supreme Command and bearing what appears to be General Ojdanic's signature?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could see General Ojdanic's signature, then I would have no reason to doubt the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could scroll up on the B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe you can ...

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is General Ojdanic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And before now you had not seen this document, I take it, and you weren't aware that General Ojdanic had sent suggestions to General Pavkovic about dealing with an order from the Joint Command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your assumption is correct. I've never seen this document before. I've never set eyes on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm curious as to how this -- how does this fit in with the principle of singleness of command? General Ojdanic, as I understand, was the highest-ranking uniformed member of the VJ, and yet here he seems to be making suggestions to his subordinate about how to deal with an order from some other entity called the Joint Command. Do you have any explanation for that? Wouldn't you normally make suggestions to a subordinate?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing unusual about making suggestions to a subordinate, that's perfectly all right, not mere suggestions, more than that even. However, I can't comment on this document. The only thing I wish to do is say how much I -- I don't believe the name used here was likely at all, Joint Command. As I know based on my military career, based on my experience, there was no such body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you familiar with or did you ever hear of a group called the -- at least in some places it's called the Inter-Departmental Staff For Combatting Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. While I was being proofed for my testimony I heard about this. I was told about the Inter-Departmental Staff For Combatting Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, but I don't know much about what their job or remit really was because I was the commander of the air force and air defence and it wasn't my job to know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So that was the first time you heard about it; you weren't aware of it in 1998 or 1999, fair?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in 1998 or in 1999. I was commander. This didn't concern me. I didn't know about it and I never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you help us with the term "Supreme Command." It's my understanding that the General Staff of the VJ, once the state of war was declared, then became during the wartime the Supreme Command Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. In wartime circumstances, the General Staff becomes the Supreme Command Staff and the Chief of Staff of the VJ becomes the head of the supreme defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or the -- that was --

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I understand that President Milosevic, who during peacetime is head of the Supreme Defence Council, during the state of war became the supreme commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, was there a body that existed during the wartime that was called the Supreme Command, do you know?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. During the war it was called the Supreme Command. As in any command where there is a command, regiment, brigade, corps, army, general staff, at all these levels, the command comprises a commander with his personnel and other bodies. A Supreme Command comprises a commander, his personnel, and other bodies attached to the staff. Therefore, Milosevic, as the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as soon as a state of war was declared became the supreme commander, supreme-wide, because he's at the top. You could call him army commander, but he's joined at the top with his staff, too, as a technical body; and together they make up the Supreme Command. This is the only way to comply with the principle of singleness of command. There is but one commander, and everyone else works for the commander and has the function of helping implement the commander's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us who were the persons by name who were part of President Milosevic's staff in the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may not be able to name them all, but the Chief of Staff was General Ojdanic with his assistants. The assistant for ground forces was Miodrag Simic. Assistant for operations and staff affairs, Obradovic, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Because if -- I know about General Ojdanic as the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, and I understand that the General Staff from peacetime became the Supreme Command Staff during wartime, perhaps with some additions. I have a question, though. You said Mr. Milosevic's staff. Were there any non-military persons on his staff that were part of the Supreme Command, any civilians that you know of?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Smiljanic, perhaps you could help me with two matters. We don't need to go into the details of all the figures again, but in answering the question about sorties and attacks and so on, you did say that there were 14.000 flights used for ground attacks and 4.000 were carried out by NATO fighter planes. Does that mean that the 4.000 carried out by the fighter planes did not involve attacks or did these also involve some form of attack?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try once again. There were 14.000 flights --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you not able to answer the question with a yes or a no?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't 4.000 attacks, it was 4.000 flights. They carried a total of six or seven strikes against the fighter planes, but they took off 4.000 times, bringing down a total of five or six planes. In one of these cases a plane eventually landed but had sustained major damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's much clearer now. Thank you. And the other matter I wanted to ask you was this: What happened to the population of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you could phrase it either more completely or more specifically. In what sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Under attack. What happened to the population as a result of the attacks in the Belgrade region?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first strikes of the first days of war, people were afraid. They were intimidated and they for the most part hid in shelters, cellars, underpasses, tunnels, or even outside the city itself. They took to the meadows surrounding Belgrade, but later on people from Belgrade formed convoys. They went to the bridges once the bridges had been targeted, and they all put paper targets on their chests saying, We, too, are a target, fire away. You could say that the people of Belgrade were left to their own devices and they had nowhere to go. The only option was to try and take shelter on the ground, which some people did. Some people stayed in underground shelters throughout the war, especially mothers with small children as well as the elderly. The youth, however, rose up against this and they led rallies and protests. They went to bridges and declared themselves to be targeted as well. There might be a more psychological reasoning behind all of this that was happening. This may be an issue for mass psychology, but this is not something that I can comment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just please clarify one thing from that answer for me. Are you saying that the convoys of people left to act as shields to protect some installations?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I said convoys, columns rather. They headed for bridges, certain facilities, city squares [Realtime transcript read in error "squad cars"], places, generally speaking, where they could assemble and which they believed might be targeted by NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll appreciate I'm trying to establish if there were large numbers of people from Belgrade headed for the border to escape the bombing.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything arising from that, Mr. Hannis, that you want to ask about? Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, a single question. Mr. Hannis asked you about all sorts of information to do with flights and attacks. You've mentioned the figure of 9.200 cases of firing and this is something to do Your Honour Judge Bonomy's question. How many missiles were fired during those operations, do you have that figure for us, sir?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I quite omitted that. A total of 22.000 tons of very powerful explosives were dropped over the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, 37.000 missiles were fired, 30 per cent of these guided missiles. I talked about the guidance systems, about GPS, about inertia-based navigation and other types of systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one translation correction I just see on the screen. Page 52 line 3, it says city squad cars, I think it was city squares. I just wanted to make sure the police wasn't involved in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I have a question in light of that last question from Mr. Visnjic and the answer because it seems inconsistent with a question I asked and got an answer if I could find it. I understood the General to say before that each firing was a single weapon -- or single missile. Page 39, line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've noted 9.200 individual weapons fired or bombs dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I have and that seems inconsistent with this last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, do you have a problem with Mr. Hannis asking for clarification of this, in view of the answer that there were 37.000 missiles fired and 22.000 tons of very powerful explosives dropped?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Hannis, you may ask for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, just to be clear, when I asked you earlier about the 9200 firings, I understood your answer to say that was each firing involved an individual missile or an individual bomb. But now in light of your answer to Mr. Visnjic that seems like that's not correct. Can you explain? Is -- each of the 9200 firings involves one or more missiles? Please explain.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE SMILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I may have misspoken. There will never be a single plane on a mission carrying a single missile or a single shell, this would be too much of a luxury that nobody can afford. There were always several bombs, the plane was carrying several bombs and dropping several bombs as a rule. On an average a single plane would carry 2.8 tons of explosives, B-52, for example, 47 tons of explosives, that's its capacity. It would approach Metohija with between 10 and 15 tons of deadly load, and they would drop MK-84, 240 kilogrammes, they would drop them from 10.000 metres altitude. So it's not as if a single attack consisted only of a single missile. Each of the planes were normally carrying on average about 2.8 tons of explosives and ordnance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Smiljanic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming here to give it. You're now free to leave us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is General Slobodan Kosovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's 007. I hope that's fine, but it's about mobilisation, it's not about the information administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, when you need private session, you'll no doubt tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Like all good 007s, he appears to have disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Efforts are being made to locate him, Mr. Visnjic, so we'll be patient for a minute or two and see if these are successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while these efforts are going on I would like to let you know that we've reduced the time for his examination; it will be significantly shorter than was announced in our 65 submission. And this is a witness who is anticipated to give testimony viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm advised that it's going to take 15 minutes or so to get the witness here. So we shall break now and we will resume at 25 minutes past 12.00, that works okay. We can sit then through to the end of the morning, and hopefully by that time the witness will be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kosovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon to everyone. My name is Slobodan Kosovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General. Could you please describe your military career in brief terms, the schools that you attended in this regard.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I am a graduate of the air defence military academy, so I am an air defence officer; after that, I completed all the highest military schools and last one was the national defence school. My last rank I retired from the rank of the lieutenant-general --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kosovac, could you please repeat the last post you held before retiral.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Executive director of the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you retired?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I am retired, but I also work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What do you do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I'm a manager in Unibroz Aviation Belgrade, it's a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what posts did you hold during the war, or rather, in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war I was the chief of the organisation department and also the deputy chief of the recruitment, conscription department, and then I became the chief -- on the 1st of April I became the chief of that administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me something about it the structure of your administration.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: My administration was in charge of organising -- of organisation, conscription, and mobilisation in the Army of Yugoslavia. It consists of the chief of the administration and two departments. The first department was department for organisation and the second one was the department for mobilisation and conscription.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In the Army of Yugoslavia were there any conscripts who were ethnic Albanians, I don't mean only in 1999 but before that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were they adequately represented in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: No. I have to say that after the break-up of the SFRY and the formation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the transformation of the JNA into the Yugoslav Army, no people, no ethnic group was adequately represented. And efforts were made to set up such an organisation and such a structure of personnel to ensure this adequate representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what did the Army of Yugoslavia do to get the Albanians into its ranks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia had two approaches. One approach was that it should engender trust in everybody in Yugoslavia so that everybody should know that this was the army of the people of Yugoslavia; and the second specific effort was to meet all the requirements of the Albanian conscripts, to favour them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please tell me, were any records kept of ethnic Albanian conscripts?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, this line of questioning, apart from the introductory part, was not indicated at all in the notification unless by saying that -- by speaking of recruitment in general it includes issues in relation to the recruitment of ethnic Albanians. We are going down another route now which is not part of the notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did you anticipate it would be about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Recruitment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The recruitment of the personnel for the VJ. The notification speaks about the rules governing the recruitment, the organisation of the recruitment, the structures in place for the recruitment. We are going into an area now as a -- which is ethnic composition of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do believe that it was indicated that the witness would be testifying. I agree with Mr. Stamp that he would be testifying about constitutional and legal provisions, but also about the role and tasks of the territorial commands and units, their composition, and organisation. So precisely that's what we're talking about, about the composition and organisation, about those things that the witness is trying to tell us. If Mr. Stamp finds that he has been prejudiced because Albanians were not listed here, I can tell you that this is just a very small part of General Kosovac's evidence, that's on one hand, and on the other we're still talking about mobilisation. I don't see how I strayed outside of -- strayed off the topic. Because that's a legal obligation of all the citizens of Serbia. The fact that now he is specifically talking about Albanians is precisely what you actually want to hear. Now we can talk about each specific ethnic group, but I believe that you're interested in issues related to the mobilisation of Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall allow you to continue as you indicate you plan to do. Mr. Stamp, if this causes specific prejudice to you, we'll address that issue as and when it arises. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, military obligation in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a general obligation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honours, I heard the term "recruitment" being mentioned. Recruitment is a much narrower term than conscription or military obligation and I did not say "regrutacija," recruitment, at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me whether records were kept of ethnic Albanian conscripts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. All conscripts in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia received a general summons to report and to be entered into the records. So this is the first part of the military obligation and then follows the recruitment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly then, military records pertain to everyone, including the Albanians by their very nature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How were records kept of the military conscripts, in what way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of this general summons the conscripts went to their military territorial commands and were entered into their records. The lists that we had in our records were compared with the lists of citizens in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and then we saw that there was this huge discrepancy between the Albanian conscripts who were on the lists and those who actually reported to be entered into the record. We repeated the summons several times and we did not apply any repressive measures in those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say that you did not apply any repressive measures, repressive measures were, in fact, envisaged by the law or some other legal instrument. Could you please tell us something else -- something more about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Well, they were envisaged in the law. Those who failed to report, summons were sent again; and if they again failed to report, then the minister of interior received a warrant for their -- to bring them in and then they were brought into the appropriate authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Why did you not apply those measures to Albanian conscripts who failed to respond to the general mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: From our discussions with the military territorial commands who had that under their purview -- in their purview and in discussions with Albanians who responded to the conscription call and the national service call, we had reliable information that Albanians from Kosovo who did respond to that call who went to do their national service, were threatened, their families were threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But in the Army of Yugoslavia there were Albanians, am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, there were Albanians, soldiers, non-commissioned officers, officers in general. All the Albanians who lived outside of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija responded and did their military obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether in those cases you took certain measures to prevent any undesirable consequences if they did respond and what were those measures?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Well, we had agreed about the measures with all the organs, and Albanians who responded to the call for recruitment and national service, we mostly complied with their requests about the selection of the unit and the location where they would serve, where they would do their national service. And we insisted that no measures should be applied against them for their failure to respond earlier. And all those measures proved to be quite efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let us move on to another topic and that's mobilisation. Could you please tell me, when can the army be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: In order to start mobilising the troops in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, some preconditions had to be met, and they were as follows. One of the states of emergency, a decision by a representative of the government -- of the prime minister, decision by the president of the state, and other measures that had to be taken. That was the point where the Chief of the General Staff had all the conditions in place to mobilise the troops, to issue an order for the mobilisation of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what documents or plans or any other kinds of documents is the Army of Yugoslavia mobilised?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: In essence, that would be the defence plan, and part of the defence plan is the general mobilisation plan. There is the plan for the mobilisation deployment, which was done in my administration for the whole army, and the plan for the mobilisation of each specific unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, it's possible that the translation is correct, but I didn't understand it right. You said that at the basis of the defence plan there is the mobilisation plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. There is the mobilisation plan which is at the base of the defence plan, it's part of it. There is the mobilisation deployment plan and the specific mobilisation plan for each specific unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When and where -- how was the mobilisation carried out in the Army of Yugoslavia in wartime?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Just before the aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, appropriate preparations were carried out because according to all indicators an aggression was imminent, we were expecting the aggression. Preparations were very complex and that's a whole different issue. After the aggression and the declaration of a state of war, the decision of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Chief of General Staff decided to mobilise commands, units, and institutions of the Army of Yugoslavia. Because of the manner of aggression he decided to carry out a selective, partial, and secret mobilisation, and he never veered from that path.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, if you could please explain to us in greater detail, what does it mean, selective, partial, and secret mobilisation, each of these terms?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia covered the entire territory of Yugoslavia. Every part of the territory was bombed, was subject to destruction, and on the basis of that the most common course would have been a general mobilisation. General mobilisation means that large capacities of the country become viable targets for the aggressor, and that is why it was decided to carry out a selective mobilisation part by part as necessary for the defence of the country because all the assets were not needed throughout the aggression. Partially, that means that only those parts that were really necessary within all that were to be mobilised. And secret mobilisation means that this was done in secret, lest the enemy should target assembly points, causing great casualties, inflicting great casualties on the Army of Yugoslavia in the most crucial point in the deployment of an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And when you say selective or partial, what does it mean? What was the order to the selection of the units were mobilisation, which units had a priority and which ones were mobilised later?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: In principle, the order is known on the basis of the nature of the units. First the command elements are mobilised, then the air defence units, then A [Realtime transcript read in error "any"] units that have to create conditions for the mobilisation of the other units and that all depended on the development, sometimes it would be engineer units, medical units, other units, depending on the requirements of the actual situation. The selective nature of the mobilisation allowed the army commanders to propose to the Chief of General Staff everything that was to be done -- what elements needed to be mobilised as the next step.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned the A composition. I don't see that in the transcript. What is the so-called A composition, which units make up this A composition?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Each army in the world has a sort of classification of its own units. A is a unit that is deployed to the greatest extent possible and can start carrying out an assignment right away and is a unit that must be mobilised before it embarks on its task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said NA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, NA, that's an abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. NA is a unit that must be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: In order to be able to carry out its fundamental task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: This doesn't preclude both units from being mobilised because A units are able to carry out their tasks but they're not able to carry on like that for long, carry on fighting like that for long.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what about the VJ before the beginning of the aggression, were there any conscripts in the army? Were there any reservists?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Based on what were those persons there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: There was several reasons for this. The general reserve is one of those reasons. This is a legal basis that provides for involvement of reservists because in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia the time when one's military term was to start was changed from 18 years of age to 21 years of age. Another reason was to train people for particular specialties that were in demand. There were reservists and the need for those reservists was high. They were called in order to be trained for particular skills and particular actions. The third reason was to keep soldiers back in the reserve once their military term is over. This was done pursuant to a decision of the president and the Chief of the General Staff. And the fourth reason was to check mobilisation readiness. This is the moment when a unit is mobilised so that its mobilisation readiness may be checked. If it's caught up in the middle of a mobilisation, then it simply continues to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many conscripts were called up and how many of those responded? What was the response to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: During the war, about 300.000 conscripts were called up. When I say "about" it's a very precise figure. It might be 300.700 or 800. The response was 90 per cent. What is typical is that at the beginning of the aggression the response was about 70 per cent, but as the aggression continued the response grew and at the very end we had units where the response rate was as high as 90 to 95 per cent and 95 to 100 per cent even.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In military terms this is a very high rate, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, this is an exceptionally high rate for any military standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was in charge of providing material support for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How did they deal with the issue of supplies, providing supplies for the units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Each unit had its own needs clearly defined. These needs were defined through war establishment. It was also clearly defined what the unit got immediately from the army in terms of material goods that were supplied to a particular unit by the army. Whatever was left and still needed to be replenished was provided by the material support of the mobilisation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And this was done through local defence ministry offices, right, local branch offices?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, those in charge of this were in the territorial command of the unit and those providing material support were local bodies of the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, could the commander of a unit on his own get certain material goods based on the list? When I refer to the list, perhaps you should explain what the list is and tell us what an officer on his own could do about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: List of goods we call them. So these are goods that are specified which a certain unit needs, and one needs to be very specific and who provides these goods, whether it's someone from the economy or an individual or the army. And then these goods were forwarded to the army. The law envisaged for the possibility -- because of the manner in which the aggression unfolded, this possibility was eventually used if the defence ministry and the body using these goods cannot bring replenishments to the unit based on the list, then the commander of a battalion can take those goods and whoever is providing the goods will be issued with a certificate to the effect that the goods were taken and used by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let us move on to a different topic. We know that volunteers were reporting to the army. Tell us when the first of these volunteers came to report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The first time was the night between the 23rd and the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did the General Staff deal with this in any special way, I mean receiving volunteers and how?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: During the night between the 23rd and 24th of May at my administration, we were aware of the fact that these volunteers reporting might be a problematic thing after all. We drew up a document of the Chief of General Staff in which we tried to deal with this issue. This document first and foremost was meant to protect units carrying out the mobilisation from any pressure exerted by these same volunteers. On the other hand, it was supposed to protect units that had not been mobilised so that their conscripts wouldn't go elsewhere. Thirdly, the aim was to prevent individuals from reporting to the army who weren't properly trained, thus putting their own lives at risk as well as those of their fellow soldiers. The fourth objective was to prevent any problematic people from reporting as volunteers, and that is why a decision was adopted on the 24th of March, 1999, to deal with all these aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, which bodies from the General Staff were involved in taking in volunteers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: My own administration was the chief body in charge, organisation, mobilisation, and military obligation, also known as the third administration. As for training, that was down to the training administration. Medical matters were something for the logistics sector. As for vetting, any volunteers that reported in terms of criminal record, this was something that the security administration was in charge of. As for deploying these units through various operative and strategic groups, that was down to my own administration. Army command were put in charge in those groups, and commanders were specifically in charge of carrying out individual assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, were there any problems about taking in volunteers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Very soon problems were noted about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How did you deal with those?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: There were two reactions. One was to issue command documents in order to consolidate this base of volunteers in a matter of about 20 days between the 24th of March and the 14th of April three orders were issued and one supplement. What was peculiar is that all these orders were used to add to the system, but not to start from scratch and build it back up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say it was added to and not -- starting from scratch and then built back up again, what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I think that the first order to regulate the intake of volunteers was essential. It provided for a normal functioning of the entire system, but this system needed adding to in order to keep the problems down to a minimum or eliminate problems altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness P1943 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before moving on, Mr. Visnjic, if you could look at line 6 of page 69. You'll see that as for -- the words there are: "As for deploying these units through various operative and strategic groups, that was done by my own administration." Now, Mr. Kosovac, what did you mean by the reference to "deploying these units"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe I actually used the word. The third administration never dealt with sending units to particular places. It was in charge of organisation and mobilisation, and organisation and mobilisation defines this, in peacetime where units are located and in wartime places where mobilisation takes place. As to where these units are actually sent, now this is operative action and this was done by staff bodies and staffs with their commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you actually said completely was that the security administration was in charge of arrangements for deploying these units through various operative -- it's unfortunate, I can't see the last words on the side of this now and it's gone from the screen. Just give me a moment. Yeah, I can see it now. What you're recorded as saying: "As for deploying these units through various operative and strategic groups, that was down to my administration." Now, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should go back to the beginning because this context is impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question was: "Which bodies from the General Staff were involved in taking in volunteers?" And you said your own administration was the chief body in charge, also known as the third administration; as for training, that was down to the training administration; medical matters were something for the logistics sector; as for vetting, any volunteers that reported in terms of criminal record, this was something that the security administration was in charge of. "As for assigning these units to various operative and strategic groups, that was down to my own administration." Now, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say "units," I said "individuals," "volunteers," sending them to the various armies and operative and strategic groups, now that was something that my administration did. Within the army they had their own organs which they deployed or assigned to various units, not units, volunteers, individuals. This is about volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, well now I have to see where I stopped. P1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you look at this document, please. It is stated that this document was produced by your administration for mobilisation, recruitment, mobilisation, and system issues. This is 1943. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You looked at this document as you were being proofed, right? Can you just tell us one thing, sir. How do you interpret this document, bearing in mind that it was issued, the body it was issued by, what was the intention of whoever produced this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: This is just to inform, to warn. As I've mentioned in my evidence so far, the first time we regulated the problem of volunteers was that order on the 24th, and until the 14th of April two other orders had been issued. That is how the command reacted to each and every mistake that was made and the command had to react in the real time. My administration was technically in charge of this. We were receiving information indicating that there were omissions and mistakes about how these volunteers were being sent out. Whenever we received a report like that - and I don't mean just us, I think every management throughout the world checks information of this kind - you check who this is in relation to, is this about all the military territorial commands or just some of those; and then based on this you draw up a document, information about specific problems and how these problems are to be overcome. Given the fact that this is the 24th, the date in question when the document was issued, and over 150.000 people had been mobilised by this time, I think this warning was a timely one, which it later proved to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's something in the transcript, page 72, line 21, it should be the 24th -- the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And when you say that over 150.000 people had been mobilised, you mean everyone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: No, just the reservists. I mean 150.000 reservists who had been mobilised by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 2 of this document in both versions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before moving to page 2, I'm having difficulty following this. This is dated the 20th of April. So you started your answer there by referring to the period between the 24th of March and the 20th of April. Did you misunderstand the date of this document? Because again you referred to the 24th at the end of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I understand correctly what this document is, and in fact I do, I drew a very clear distinction between a document issuing a command and a document informing or warning somebody about something. The command responds in real time to any problems that are noted. You saw that we dealt with those problems in four documents that dealt with the problem of volunteers. When we were informed about some conduct that appeared to be of a systematic nature, we checked this information with the military territorial commands, we analysed who this -- these problems referred to, and when we decided that this was a common problem, we drafted a document informing and warning everyone in order to avoid any such problems in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can help me with some specific questions. You said that 150.000 reservists had been mobilised by this time. What was the date by which you had mobilised 150.000 reservists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this letter here is dated the 20th, so we are four weeks into the war by this time. And you were receiving reports of paramilitary groups and unsatisfactory volunteers and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My organs responded only to individuals because we admitted only individuals, no groups, in particular, not paramilitary groups. Every individual was processed as such, as an individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This document in its second paragraph says: "There was no organised processing of the volunteers in the Bubanj Potok PC," which presumably is reception centre, "in the beginning, instead" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: " -- Instead they were brought together and transferred to the 3rd Army reception centre, often with no agreement or coordination. Most often these were paramilitary groups that had been formed before, and among their forces they had a number of volunteer unfit for military service," and then there's a number of reasons given. So were these the reports you were getting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were the reports that we were getting immediately before this document was drafted, but I'm telling you every individual was processed individually so that any assumptions about groups are just that, assumptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let us go back to the last page of this document in B/C/S, that's page 2 in English. Could you please look at the last paragraph of this document. It reads: "On the basis of all of the above, take measures to eliminate the problems and oversights that were noted and to entirely secure the execution of the order issued by the chief of the Supreme Command Staff," we have the number, dated the 14th of April, 1999. Could you please comment on the last paragraph with the fact who these documents, or rather, who this notification or warning was addressed to.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: You can see right away that this warning, this information, was addressed to three types of units down there and agencies. First of all, to the army commands that were in command of the military territorial commands, and then pursuant to this order they were able to define their command actions. Second --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 3 in the English because this part the addressees are listed on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Please proceed, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Second, to the training administration because it was in charge of training; and thirdly, to all military territorial commands as a technical aspect of this problem, not down the chain of command but as a technical warning or instruction as to how they should do their job. This type of distribution is considered to be highly efficient when there isn't enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what would be the regular distribution or manner in which this would be conveyed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Only to the army commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you remember or do you have information about the number of volunteers, total number in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I remember quite clearly the basic framework, around 6.000 volunteers reported, 20 per cent were immediately sent off from the reception centres, they were not admitted, 20 per cent were soon sent off from their units, and the rest remained to the end, doing their job until the end. I remember quite clearly that about 150 foreigners came to the country to join as volunteers. We used 140 of them. We didn't admit a small number. I remember quite clearly that we had demands from abroad for about 10.000 volunteers to come in and to put -- place themselves at the disposal of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did you do the recruitment and reception of soldiers during the war, admission of soldiers? We're talking about another topic, we're talking about the recruitment now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Well, probably you meant doing national service or admission of persons doing their national service?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Well, recruits, people who were already recruited came to do the national service. We did not call-up people to do their national service during the war because we estimated that our personnel strength is sufficient to repel the aggression. We made such a proposal to the Chief of General Staff, and he agreed. We drafted plans and we assessed that if the aggression should go on that sometime in September or October we would start calling up recruits to do their national service.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, could you please tell me, high school students in military schools and students were also sent home. What was the basis for that decision?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the regulations in force and the rules for the mobilisation of the army, it is quite clearly defined which students of the military high schools and students from military academies should be assigned as soon as the army is mobilised and as soon as the state is at war. The Chief of the General Staff assessed that the time was not right for the high school, military high school students and military academy students to be engaged on the basis of our proposal and the proposal of the training administration which was in charge of running the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now that we're talking about the training administration, what kinds of training are there, General, in the army? Who is being trained?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Well, for all intents and purposes there are two types of training in the army. One is the training an individual and training of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what was your assessment of the training level of the individuals; and if you can, perhaps also tell us about the units in that time-period right at the beginning of the war. Let us start with the individuals first.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Well, I am competent to answer that question through the prism of mobilisation and let me give you the following answer. No military conscript in the army was ever used in the army if they had not been trained. So all the conscripts had undergone training. Second, through the verification of combat-readiness no unit was failed in terms of its level of training; in other words, every unit was assessed to be satisfactory in terms of its training level. And third, the Army of Yugoslavia was never happy at that time with the level of training of its units because we knew that we could always do better, that we could do more, and that's what we concentrated our efforts on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are there any objective reasons why the level of training may have been lower in some units and what might those reasons be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Well, there are many reasons. Let me give you just a few of the most salient ones. External reasons were the following. The state had been under a blockade for a long period of time, and that is why it was difficult to obtain and to have proper teaching aids. This caused an economic crisis and it was difficult to allocate funding for training. Next, the situation in the environment of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was among the most difficult in the world. There was civil war in its neighbouring countries to the south, the obstruction by the separatists and constant threat of war. And third, we knew that we had to find the best possible solution and in that period immediately before the aggression and in the course of the aggression the 2.000 model was at work, that was a plan, for the transformation and reform of the Army of Yugoslavia. Let me just note here that those transformations and reforms that had taken place before were aimed at reducing the number of units and the personnel strength in the Army of Yugoslavia, both in its peacetime and wartime establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You referred in that answer to civil war in your neighbouring countries to the south. To which countries were you referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the civil war in the neighbouring countries, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I was talking about the south of Serbia as a separate issue, Kosovo and Metohija, southern Serbia, Kosovo and Metohija, that's all part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this answer relates to the period up to 1995, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the period up to 1999. That's the whole period of preparations that takes six years from the moment of transformation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we listen to the audio-recording, because I'm sure about what the witness said about what you remarked on, I think that it will be quite clear. I think that he was quite clear in his audio-recording, and there probably was some summarizing in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you recall how many units were mobilised at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Well, I have the information as to how many units were mobilised throughout the war. About 150 units were fully mobilised in the army, partially mobilised were 140 units, and about 200 commands and institutions were not mobilised at all but they worked in their peacetime organisation during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information about the 3rd Army, what the situation was there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Well, the situation was approximately the same, about 40 units were fully mobilised and about 36 units were partially mobilised, plus/minus one, two units, but that's reliable information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: During the war were new commands and units and institutions established?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. During the war, the war always produces the formation of others. We issued about 25 orders from the Chief of General Staff to set up new commands, units, and institutions of the army, and they regulated the formation of about 40 new units, commands, and institutions, most of these were units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you know or you probably know something about the establishment of the military territorial detachment at the military department in -- military district in Pristina -- military territorial detachment that was supposed to be composed of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Of Albanian -- ethnic Albanian conscripts?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I know that during the war the only newly formed detachment was this one, I think it was the 9th Military Territorial Detachment. The assistant Chief of General Staff, General Matovic, at a meeting of the collegium of our sector notified us about the demand and the proposal of the 3rd Army command. He notified us why -- what was the purpose of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The purpose was to establish a single unit where the officers, non-commissioned and commissioned officers and soldiers would be Albanians, and the purpose was to increase the trust of the Albanian population in Kosovo for the Army of Yugoslavia. On the basis of the situation assessment, we proposed to general, who was the assistant Chief of General Staff, that this be a military territorial unit, that it be a detachment, and if a greater number of such conscripts should report, that we could spread those units in the most -- in the best possible way because that was the most favourable way in which they could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And what was done next by the General Staff in this regard, did appropriate -- were the appropriate documents issued were appropriate organisational preconditions put in place and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. The Chief of General Staff fully accepted the proposal, and all the documents were drafted necessary for the setting up of the 9th Military Territorial Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the detachment was eventually set up; if so, did it start functioning at any point?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I do know that. When the time came to report that its establishment was done, the feedback we received was that they had failed, so we scrapped all the documents. The commander of the Pristina military district at a briefing told me in detail why this detachment had never been set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's move on to a different topic now, it's about the relations between the army and the MUP during subordination and resubordination. My question: During the war was any unit of the MUP resubordinated to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Not a single unit of the MUP was ever part of the establishment of the VJ or, for that matter, defined as such even in theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What was the fundamental reason for what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: We would underline this quite often. The fundamental reasons were, these are two entirely different systems, the army and the MUP. They have different command systems. They have different recruitment systems. They have different purposes and goals. They have different logistics. They have different deployment conditions, and they can never be unified under a single banner, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, demands were made to resubordinate, weren't they? What was the gist of those demands?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: In essence it was about interpreting the word "resubordination" and what exactly this implied. There were a great many problems in dealing with specific problems. The Law on Defence defines this really well. When a unit of the VJ and a unit of the MUP worked together, who exactly is in charge of this operation and what does one do. In essence, action is coordinated between the VJ and the MUP, and in combat, in armed combat, it is the army that is in charge of coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, defined like this, resubordination or coordination, whatever we choose to call it, at which level is this sort of cooperation implemented?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: A coordination. The body in charge of coordination defines the basic elements, the initial elements, for guidance in terms of this coordination. The army commands issue assignments to their own units. Coordination itself and the hot [Realtime transcript read in error "hard"] line that exists between the MUP and a particular VJ unit is maintained at the level of battalions and brigades at the level where combat activities are carried out. It's normally done like this: There is a MUP representative at the command post of the unit in question and then issues are dealt with as they come.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zecevic is telling me about page 83, line 6, it says "hard line," whereas the General said "hot line" and I think there is a definitely distinction and this affects the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was also translated as "hot line" orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we'll be going through some documents at the end of your evidence so we'll not be wasting any time now. Even at this level that you've just described, were there any practical problems, the level that we can henceforth refer to as the hot line, level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Most frequently problems did occur at that level. Coordination problems and such-like never occur at the highest level, at the level of state, at the level of the actual coordinating body. It's always at a stage or at a level where this is actually implemented that problems occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I'll be asking you to look at a series of documents now. 3D751 is the first of these. The document is dated the 19th of March; it was issued by the VJ General Staff. General, can you please say this. In real language what does paragraph 1 of the document state, start immediately with: "Preparations for the mobilisation of the 252nd corps unit ..."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: This is a textbook preparation order that any military officer expecting that a certain issue would occur in real terms should issue. It means what it says: "Carry out preparations ..." What does that mean? A unit is envisaged to be mobilised. In this case the 252nd Armoured Brigade, this is an A unit, it's classified as an A unit. It's meant to launch fast into action wherever an attack by the enemy is expected. It must bring its lists up-to-date, it must prepare all its units, it must be prepared for all its commitments, and it must be prepared to launch into action in no time at all because this is the unit carrying out that assignment. As for territorial commands, those that the army is in charge of, this means that they should check their lists, conscripts, check their messages or couriers and be ready as soon as an order comes to start mobilising. This is one of the regular preparation orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 3D749.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Another order by the Chief of the General Staff, the date is the 23rd of March, 1999. Look at paragraph 1, please. This is the continuation, right? Can you comment, General, what is that -- what is it that's being ordered here by the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: If you look at the date you see that it was actually produced on the 22nd, on the eve of the aggression, and the 23rd is the date that it was actually dispatched. In practical terms you see that four days had elapsed since the previous order and all the preparations had probably been completed. So this is yet another caution that preparations should continue, that no one should start relaxing who was within the system, because unfortunately on that day it was confirmed that there would be an aggression against the SFRY and that orders were to start being carried out for mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let us now move on to P1741.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We believe that counsel actually used that number but it's impossible to tell because of the background noise in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that 1741?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1741. The previous one was 3D749.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is the order on mobilisation of the 2nd of April, 1999, in this case the 2nd Army. Can you please comment. I see that this order precedes the order of the Supreme Command Staff also on the 2nd of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: To the extent I can tell it's the 3rd Army we're looking at here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak up, the interpreters can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I was talking about at the beginning. The Chief of the General Staff opted for selective, partial and secret mobilisation and this is an specific order that he has now issued to mobilise units. One can see that the army command -- perhaps we should turn to the next page. Yes. The army command here deals with everything that it is in charge of and it encompasses everything in this order and regulates it for everyone who will be involved in this mobilisation. So this is an order from the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now go to 3D750.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is an order. You spoke about soldiers who had completed their military term but were held back. Can you please comment on this order and especially the reason why these soldiers were held back. The date is the 15th of March, it's another order by the VJ General Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: To all practical intents, this is an order that was based on a decision of the president of the FRY, and this was drafted by the Chief of the General Staff and was forwarded to all the units that all the soldiers should be held back as military conscripts, also those whose term had expired. What is behind this order? We all know that once someone's military term expires, this is normally the best soldier around because he's well-trained, perfectly fit, and there are good teams who have now worked together for quite some time. On the other hand, the problem relating to manpower levels in the army was a burning issue at the time already. On the other hand, we know that the aggression spread in a lightning-quick manner and it was expected that it would be launched at any time. For whatever the president took this decision and the Chief of the General Staff implemented it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This was a public decision, was it not, or a secret one, General, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: This is not the sort of decision that you publish. You can see that it says: "Strictly confidential." This sent to the commands of all units and institutions so that all those who should know know about this, but this is not some sort of a public proclamation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure -- I have about -- well, if I tell you now, I would be lying to you, but I think 15 minutes, and I mean to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid there will be another case here this afternoon, so we have to move out. Mr. Kosovac, we have to bring our sitting to an end at this stage because another case sits in this court in the afternoon. That means you have to come here to continue with your evidence, that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Overnight it's very important that you have no discussion with anyone about any of the evidence in the case. You can discuss whatever you like with whomever you like, as long as there is absolutely no discussion about the evidence. Now, would you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
